title: Record every echo the host sends

blocks.text: Some hosts check a quiet link by sending echoes of their own: an 0800 that your client must answer with an 0810. `EchoResponder` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/EchoResponder.java` does that job as a request listener on the client's QMUX. Its class comment shows the `<request-listener>` element that deploys it.

Last week the host's operations team reported that your client had stopped answering their echoes for an hour. Your log had nothing on it, so nobody could say whether the echoes arrived, whether replies went out, or what failed. Operations now want one entry per echo in the node's log, under the listener's realm, that shows what came in and what went back, or why nothing did.
Finish the two methods marked `TODO`: `setLogger` and `answer`. About ten lines in total.
The tests give the listener its logger the way Q2 does, then hand it echoes from a link that records the replies and, in one test, fails to send.

cases.says: an echo from the host is answered with an 0810 and recorded in the log
the entry reaches the logger and realm Q2 gave the listener, because the event's source is the listener's Log
each echo is one entry holding both the echo and the reply
an echo whose reply fails to go out still gets its entry, with the reason, because the entry is written whatever happened

origin.section: 8.2 An Event Goes to Its Source's Logger, and a Channel Without One Writes Nothing

concepts: A log event holds one piece of work, is created when the work starts and is written once in finally, so it keeps request, answer, duration and outcome together even when the work fails.
Logger.log delivers an event to its source's logger: an event without a source goes to Q2, and an event from a Log or channel that has no logger goes nowhere.
